extracted.intended_audience: AI/NLP researchers, patent data scientists, and IP practitioners interested in using USPTO open data
extracted.subtask_short: using USPTO data for AI research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for applying AI & NLP techniques to USPTO patent archives and for constructing patent-derived datasets and benchmarks to advance both IP practice and AI research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal requirement to disseminate patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO is required by law to disseminate most nonprovisional patent applications and granted patents (35 U.S.C. § 122(b); 37 C.F.R. § 1.11(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent data from the USPTO is publicly accessible and can be used as a substrate for research and commercial applications; agency dissemination obligations are the legal basis for publicly available patent corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary operational AI application areas at the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationally, the USPTO focuses on two critical areas of AI application: prior art search and patent classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects aiming to assist IP administration should prioritize these two areas—improving examiner-facing search systems and automating assignment of classification symbols/claim indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use representation learning to produce semantically meaningful embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation learning and related techniques can produce semantically meaningful embeddings of language, graphs, images, and even proteins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply embedding techniques to patent texts, figures, and structured data to surface semantically relevant prior art and support downstream tasks (search, clustering, similarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage patent classification workflow (CPC + claim indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO currently classifies patents using a two-stage process: first assign a set of Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) symbols to each patent; second determine the subset of CPC symbols ('claim indicators') associated with claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI systems for classification should reflect this two-stage workflow; the USPTO has deployed ML to assign claim indicators and is augmenting models to assign full CPC sets, typically trained on annotated USPTO patent data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search tools should support natural-language queries and surface diverse document types
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor-facing tools (e.g., the Inventor Search Assistant) surface published applications, non-patent literature (NPL), and foreign patent documents, and use machine learning to offer initial overviews from natural language queries alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design prior-art search interfaces that reduce entry barriers (no steep query syntax) by supporting plain-language queries and aggregating USPTO, NPL, and foreign sources to benefit independent and early-stage inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use USPTO data for patent landscaping and technology field classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A common patent analysis task is to sort patent documents into specific fields of technology or business applications ('patent landscaping'); deep learning has been applied to this task using USPTO data for training and as target documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage supervised and deep learning classification on USPTO corpora to build patent-landscaping tools; use curated labels and CPC metadata where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI Patent Dataset construction: detect AI presence and component technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO’s AI Patent Dataset identifies the presence of AI in over 13 million U.S. patent documents and further sorts them into one of eight component technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dataset was created by training a recurrent neural network in a semi-supervised manner to distinguish between positive and negative examples—implying semi-supervised RNN approaches are appropriate for large-scale concept-detection in patent corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract prosecution history (Office actions) via ML/NLP for analytics
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO’s Office Action Research Dataset comprises a relational database of key elements from 4.4 million Office actions, created using machine learning and NLP techniques to systematically extract information from Office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history is an often-overlooked data source for patent analytics; use automated extraction to make examiner-issued rejections and other prosecution artifacts accessible for empirical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize data quality and diversity when building LLM training corpora
rubrics_metrics.description: Early large language model datasets were lightly curated; Gao et al. compiled a dataset prioritizing both data quality and diversity, combining background sections of millions of U.S. patents with other sources to form 'The Pile'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For language-model training and evaluation, explicitly select and curate patent-derived text for quality and diversity rather than ingesting raw dumps without filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include patent background sections, and consider full specifications and prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: Background sections of patents were used successfully in large-scale LM datasets, but future datasets could include full patent specifications or prosecution history documents (e.g., Office actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full specifications and prosecution histories are recommended as promising sources of scientific and legal reasoning examples not easily found elsewhere; include these to better capture domain-specific discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create classification benchmarks using CPC annotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Public USPTO data and CPC annotations have been used to create text classification benchmarks (patent classification as a quintessential multiclass challenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CPC labels and large-scale patent corpora to build standardized benchmarks for evaluating classification models and comparing architectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct semantic-similarity benchmarks via phrase extraction and manual rating
rubrics_metrics.description: One method for a semantic similarity benchmark: extract phrases from patent documents, generate facially similar phrases, and manually rate semantic similarity of each phrase pair on a five-point scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine automated generation of candidate pairs with human annotation (Likert-style) and evaluate models using appropriate correlation metrics (e.g., Pearson correlation, as used in a Kaggle competition achieving 87.8% top correlation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refashion patent data into AI research benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO is interested in fostering efforts to refashion patent data into valuable AI research benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing datasets or benchmarks from patent data, document provenance, labeling methodology, and evaluation metrics so the datasets can serve both IP-focused applications and general AI research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use curated, annotated USPTO corpora to train practical IP tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO and commercial developers have used publicly-available USPTO data to train AI models that provide capabilities to IP software products (e.g., claim-indicator assignment, portfolio intelligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For production tools aimed at practitioners, train models on annotated USPTO data and validate on use-cases such as examiner search augmentation, claim scope identification, and portfolio analytics.
